goals: Classify an animal by organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom and segmentation
List the distinguishing features and two examples of each non-chordate phylum
Assign an invertebrate to its phylum from its features

slides.heading: Animal Kingdom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how zoologists sort over a million species, and the ten non-chordate phyla.

visual.alt: Flow showing the four levels of organisation in animals from cellular to organ system

slides.narration: Animals are sorted by their basic body plan, not by size or habitat. The first question is how the cells are organised: as loose cells, as tissues, as organs or as organ systems. Further questions are about symmetry, germ layers and the body cavity.

slides.heading: Symmetry of the body
slides.body_md: Animals may be **asymmetrical**, **radially symmetrical** or **bilaterally symmetrical**.

slides.narration: A sponge has no plane that cuts it into equal halves. A sea anemone can be halved by any plane through its central axis. A worm can be halved along one plane only, giving a left and a right half, and it also has a head end and a tail end.

slides.heading: Levels of organisation and germ layers
slides.body_md: The embryo of a **diploblastic** animal has two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm; a **triploblastic** animal also has mesoderm. Of 10 non-chordate phyla listed here, 7 are triploblastic and 2 are diploblastic; sponges have no true germ layers.

rows: Cells are loosely arranged; no true tissues
Cells doing the same work are grouped; no organs
Organs work together in a system

visual.alt: Table of levels of organisation with example phyla

slides.narration: In sponges, cells are not grouped into tissues. In cnidarians and ctenophores, cells are grouped into tissues. In flatworms the tissues form organs, and in annelids and higher groups the organs form systems. The number of germ layers is another basis: two layers or three.

slides.heading: Body cavity: acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate
slides.body_md: A **coelom** is a body cavity lined by **mesoderm**. In an **acoelomate** there is no cavity; in a **pseudocoelomate** the cavity is not fully lined by mesoderm; in a **coelomate** it is. Arthropods have a blood-filled **haemocoel**.

slides.narration: Look at the position of the mesoderm. If it fills the space, the animal is acoelomate. If a cavity lies between mesoderm and gut with no mesoderm around the gut, it is pseudocoelomate. If mesoderm lines the cavity on both sides, it is a true coelom.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classify an animal
slides.body_md: An animal is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and pseudocoelomate. Which phylum is it?
bullets: Bilateral and triploblastic: not Porifera, Cnidaria or Ctenophora.
Acoelomate bilateral animals are **Platyhelminthes**, so the pseudocoelom rules them out.
A pseudocoelom with a complete gut and a cuticle fits **Nematoda**.

visual.alt: Worked table assigning phyla from symmetry, germ layers and coelom

slides.narration: Eliminate step by step. Bilateral and triploblastic removes the first three phyla. The kind of body cavity then separates flatworms, roundworms and arthropods. A pseudocoelom points to the roundworms, the phylum Nematoda.

slides.heading: Segmentation
slides.body_md: **Metamerism** is the division of the body into repeated segments, each with a copy of some organs.

rows: Rings; each has nephridia and setae
External segments often fused into head, thorax and abdomen
Internal, in the muscles and vertebral column

visual.alt: Table of segmentation in annelids, arthropods and chordates

slides.narration: Only two of the 10 non-chordate phyla listed here are truly segmented, annelids and arthropods. In an earthworm the segments show on the outside as rings and are also repeated inside. Chordates show segmentation in their muscles and backbone.

slides.body_md: **Porifera**: asymmetrical, cellular level, body with **pores** (ostia), a central **spongocoel**, an **osculum**, **choanocytes**, and a skeleton of **spicules or spongin**.

slides.heading: Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes and Nematoda
slides.body_md: Three more phyla, with different body plans.

rows: Radial, diploblastic; eight rows of ciliated comb plates; bioluminescence; no stinging cells
Flat, bilateral, acoelomate; hooks and suckers in parasites; flame cells; no anus
Round, pseudocoelomate; complete gut; cuticle; sexes separate

visual.alt: Table of three phyla: Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes and Nematoda with features and examples

slides.narration: Ctenophores swim with eight rows of comb plates and many glow in the dark. Flatworms are flat, have flame cells for excretion, and a gut with a single opening. Roundworms are cylindrical, with a complete gut and separate male and female animals.

slides.heading: Annelida and Mollusca
slides.body_md: Annelids are **segmented**, with a closed blood system; molluscs have a **soft body in a shell**, a **mantle** and a **radula**.

rows: Segmented body, coelomate, setae or parapodia, nephridia, closed circulation
Soft body, muscular foot, mantle and often a shell, radula, open circulation in most

visual.alt: Table of Annelida and Mollusca with features and examples

slides.narration: An earthworm has rings, bristles called setae and nephridia for excretion. A snail has a muscular foot, a shell secreted by the mantle, and a rasping organ called the radula. Molluscs are the second largest phylum.

slides.heading: Arthropoda, Echinodermata and Hemichordata
slides.body_md: Arthropods are the **largest phylum**; echinoderms have a **water vascular system**; hemichordates are **worm-like with a proboscis**.

rows: Jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, haemocoel, open circulation, Malpighian tubules in insects
Spiny skin, radial adult but bilateral larva, water vascular system, tube feet
Proboscis, collar and trunk; gill slits; open circulation

visual.alt: Table of Arthropoda, Echinodermata and Hemichordata with features and examples

slides.narration: Arthropods have jointed legs and a hard exoskeleton of chitin, and more than two thirds of all named animals belong to this phylum. Echinoderms use a water vascular system with tube feet to move. Hemichordates are marine worms with a body in three parts.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sort a pond sample
slides.body_md: A net brings up 48 small animals: 6 flatworms, 4 roundworms, 10 annelids, 14 molluscs and 14 arthropods. How many are coelomate, how many segmented, and what share are flatworms?
bullets: Coelomate: annelids and molluscs, 10 + 14 = **24**.
Segmented: annelids and arthropods, 10 + 14 = **24**.
Flatworms: 6 ÷ 48 × 100 = **12.5 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the pond sample with coelom and segmentation

slides.narration: First decide the body cavity of each group. Annelids and molluscs are coelomate. Then decide segmentation: only annelids and arthropods. Finally turn the flatworm count into a share of the whole sample. Notice that arthropods have a haemocoel, not a true coelom.

slides.heading: Quick check: pond sample
slides.body_md: In the pond sample, how many animals are segmented?
slides.narration: Quick check. Add the two segmented phyla.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Basis of classification: level of organisation, symmetry, number of germ layers, body cavity and segmentation.
Porifera: asymmetrical, choanocytes, osculum; Cnidaria: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa; Ctenophora: comb plates.
Platyhelminthes: flat, flame cells; Nematoda: round, pseudocoelom, complete gut.
Annelida: segmented; Mollusca: mantle, radula; Arthropoda: jointed appendages, chitin.
Echinodermata: water vascular system; Hemichordata: proboscis, collar and trunk.

visual.alt: Summary table of body plans and phyla

slides.narration: To recap: ten non-chordate phyla are sorted by organisation, symmetry, germ layers, body cavity and segmentation. For each phylum remember one defining feature, such as choanocytes in sponges or the radula in molluscs.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **at least five features and two examples** for a phylum when asked.
Say **haemocoel** for arthropods, **pseudocoelom** for roundworms and **true coelom** for annelids.
Do not call echinoderms radial without adding "**the adult**": the larva is bilateral.
Write scientific names in **italics or underlined**, with the genus capitalised.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give five features and two examples for each phylum. Use the correct word for the body cavity. Say that only the adult echinoderm is radial. And underline scientific names.

goals: State the fundamental features of chordates and distinguish the three subphyla

slides.heading: Chordata
slides.body_md: Part 2 — animals with a notochord, from lancelets to mammals.

visual.alt: Flow from phylum Chordata to its three subphyla

slides.narration: Phylum Chordata contains three subphyla. Two of them are small marine groups of animals without a backbone. The third, the vertebrates, includes fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, all with a backbone.

slides.heading: Fundamental features of chordates
slides.body_md: Every chordate has, at some stage, a **notochord**, a **dorsal hollow nerve cord**, **pharyngeal gill slits** and a **post-anal tail**; the heart is **ventral**.

slides.narration: The notochord is a rod of mesoderm on the back side. Above it lies a hollow nerve cord. The pharynx has slits that open to the outside, and the tail extends beyond the anus. Non-chordates have a solid nerve cord on the belly side.

slides.heading: Chordates compared with non-chordates
slides.body_md: Five points of difference help to tell a chordate from an invertebrate.

visual.alt: Table comparing chordates and non-chordates

slides.narration: The two groups differ in the position of the nerve cord and the heart as well as in having a notochord. In chordates the nerve cord is hollow and on the back. In annelids and arthropods it is solid and on the belly.

slides.heading: Three subphyla
slides.body_md: The notochord decides the subphylum.

rows: Whole length of the body, throughout life
Replaced by a vertebral column in the adult

visual.alt: Table of the three subphyla of Chordata with notochord and example

slides.narration: In sea squirts the notochord is found only in the tail of the tadpole-like larva. In the lancelet it stays from head to tail through life. In vertebrates it is replaced by a backbone made of vertebrae.

slides.heading: Quick check: subphyla
slides.body_md: In which subphylum is the notochord present only in the larval tail?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of a sea squirt.

slides.heading: Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes
slides.body_md: Fishes are **aquatic**, breathe with **gills** and have a **two-chambered heart**.

rows: Jawless, sucking mouth, no scales, no paired fins, gill slits; marine, migrate to fresh water to breed
Cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, gill slits without cover, no air bladder, internal fertilisation
Bony skeleton, operculum over the gills, air bladder, scales, external fertilisation

visual.alt: Table of the three classes of fishes with features and examples

slides.narration: Lampreys and hagfishes are jawless and have a round sucking mouth. Sharks and rays have a skeleton of cartilage and must keep swimming because they lack an air bladder. Bony fishes have a gill cover, the operculum, and an air bladder that gives buoyancy.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting gill slits
slides.body_md: A lamprey has 7 pairs of gill slits and a dogfish shark has 5 pairs. How many slits does each animal have, and what is the difference?
bullets: Difference: 14 − 10 = **4** slits.

visual.alt: Worked table of gill slits in a lamprey and a shark

slides.narration: Gill slits occur in pairs, one on each side, so double the number of pairs. A lamprey has seven pairs, which is fourteen slits. A dogfish shark has five pairs, which is ten, so the lamprey has four more.

slides.heading: Amphibia and Reptilia
slides.body_md: Amphibians live in water and on land; reptiles are fully terrestrial with a **dry, scaly skin**.

rows: Moist skin without scales, three-chambered heart, cloaca, external fertilisation, eggs in water, tympanum
Dry cornified skin with scales, usually three-chambered heart (crocodiles have four), internal fertilisation, shelled eggs on land

visual.alt: Table of Amphibia and Reptilia with features and examples

slides.narration: A frog has a moist skin that helps in breathing and lays its eggs in water. A lizard has dry scaly skin that prevents water loss and lays shelled eggs on land. Both have a three-chambered heart, except crocodiles, which have four chambers.

slides.heading: Aves and Mammalia
slides.body_md: Birds and mammals are **warm-blooded**, with a **four-chambered heart**.

rows: Feathers, wings, beak, air-filled bones, oviparous, no sweat glands
Mammary glands, hair, external ears, diaphragm, mostly viviparous; Ornithorhynchus lays eggs

visual.alt: Table of Aves and Mammalia with features and examples

slides.narration: Birds have feathers, wings and bones with air spaces, which suit flight. Mammals suckle their young with milk from mammary glands and have hair. The platypus is an egg-laying mammal.

slides.heading: Hearts of vertebrates
slides.body_md: The number of chambers rises from **two** in fishes to **three** in amphibians and most reptiles and **four** in birds and mammals.

Warm-blooded animals are birds and mammals: 8 + 2 = **10**.

slides.body_md: Compare the classes on covering, heart and body temperature.

Mammals: mammary glands and hair; birds: feathers.

notes.title: Animal Kingdom — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Basis of classification
sections.body_md:
Animals are classified by their **fundamental body plan**, using features that are shared by whole groups.

- **Levels of organisation.** *Cellular* level: cells loosely arranged, as in sponges. *Tissue* level: cells doing the same work are grouped into tissues, as in cnidarians and ctenophores. *Organ* level: tissues form organs, as in flatworms. *Organ-system* level: organs work together in systems, as in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.
- **Symmetry.** *Asymmetrical* (no plane divides the body into equal halves; most sponges); *radial* (any plane through the central axis gives equal halves; cnidarians, ctenophores, adult echinoderms); *bilateral* (only one plane gives left and right halves, with a head end; flatworms to chordates).
- **Germ layers.** *Diploblastic* animals have an outer **ectoderm** and an inner **endoderm** with an undifferentiated layer, the **mesoglea**, between them (cnidarians, ctenophores). *Triploblastic* animals have a third layer, the **mesoderm**, between them (flatworms onwards).
- **Body cavity (coelom).** A **coelom** is a cavity lined by mesoderm. **Acoelomate:** no cavity (flatworms). **Pseudocoelomate:** a cavity not fully lined by mesoderm (roundworms). **Coelomate:** a true coelom (annelids, molluscs, echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates). **Haemocoelomate:** the coelom is reduced and the body cavity is filled with blood, the **haemocoel** (arthropods).
- **Segmentation (metamerism).** The body is divided into repeated segments with a repeat of some organs: annelids (external and internal), arthropods, and chordates (in muscles and vertebral column).
- **Other features** used at lower levels: the type of digestive tract (complete or incomplete), the circulatory system (open or closed), and the presence of a notochord.

*Where books differ.* Some books call molluscs and arthropods "coelomate" and treat the haemocoel as a reduced coelom; the ISC syllabus lists "haemocoelomate" as a type, so the notes follow that. Whether sponges are "cellular" or "diploblastic" also varies; sponges are treated here as the cellular grade.

sections.heading: 2. Non-chordates I: Porifera, Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda
sections.body_md:
**Porifera (sponges).** Mostly marine, asymmetrical, **cellular level**. The body wall has many pores (**ostia**) and a central cavity (**spongocoel**) that opens by the **osculum**; the cavity is lined by flagellated **choanocytes** (collar cells), which create a water current. Water brings food and oxygen and carries away wastes. A skeleton of **spicules** or **spongin** supports the body. Sponges are hermaphrodite (eggs and sperm in one animal) with **indirect development** through a free-swimming larva. Examples: Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia.

**Cnidaria (coelenterates).** Aquatic, radial, **diploblastic**, tissue level. They bear stinging cells, **cnidoblasts** (cnidocytes), on the tentacles for anchorage, defence and capturing prey. The **gastrovascular cavity** has a single opening, the **hypostome**, which is both mouth and anus. Two body forms: the sessile, cylindrical **polyp** (*Hydra*, *Adamsia*) and the free-swimming umbrella-shaped **medusa** (*Aurelia*). Some show both forms in the life cycle, as in *Obelia* (**metagenesis**). Examples: Hydra, Aurelia, Physalia.

**Ctenophora (comb jellies).** Marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level, with **eight external rows of ciliated comb plates** for locomotion. **Bioluminescence** is common. No cnidoblasts; fertilisation is external and development indirect. Examples: Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana.

**Platyhelminthes (flatworms).** Dorsoventrally flattened, bilaterally symmetrical, **triploblastic, acoelomate**, organ level. Many are endoparasites, with **hooks and suckers**. They excrete and osmoregulate through **flame cells**; there is no anus in most. Some, such as *Planaria*, have great powers of **regeneration**. Examples: Taenia, Fasciola, Planaria.

**Nematoda (Aschelminthes, roundworms).** Circular in cross-section, bilateral, triploblastic, **pseudocoelomate**, organ-system level. The alimentary canal is **complete** with a muscular pharynx, the body is covered by a **cuticle**, sexes are separate (**dioecious**), and females are usually longer than males. Many are parasites. Examples: Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma.

sections.heading: 3. Non-chordates II: Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Echinodermata, Hemichordata
sections.body_md:
**Annelida.** Aquatic or terrestrial, bilateral, triploblastic, **coelomate**, with **metameric segmentation**. Body surface divided into rings; locomotory structures are **setae** (earthworm) or **parapodia** (*Nereis*). A closed circulatory system, **nephridia** for excretion and osmoregulation, a ventral solid nerve cord. *Nereis* is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Examples: Nereis, Pheretima, Hirudinaria.

**Mollusca.** The second largest phylum. Soft, unsegmented body with a head, a muscular **foot** and a visceral hump covered by the **mantle**, which usually secretes a calcareous **shell**. Gills (**ctenidia**) lie in the mantle cavity; the mouth has a file-like **radula**; circulation is open in most; excretion is by kidneys. Mostly dioecious. Examples: Pila, Octopus, Pinctada.

**Arthropoda.** The largest phylum, with over two thirds of named species. Bilateral, triploblastic, **haemocoelomate**, segmented, with **jointed appendages** and a **chitinous exoskeleton**. Respiration by gills, book gills, book lungs or **tracheae**; **open circulation**; excretion by **Malpighian tubules** in insects. Sensory organs include antennae and compound eyes; usually dioecious with internal fertilisation. Examples: Palaemon, Apis, Limulus.

**Echinodermata.** Marine; **spiny skin** over a calcareous endoskeleton; **radial symmetry in the adult** but a bilateral larva; coelomate. The **water vascular system** with **tube feet** helps in locomotion, capture of food and respiration; there is no excretory system. Examples: Asterias, Echinus, Antedon.

**Hemichordata.** Worm-like marine animals with a body of **proboscis, collar and trunk**; open circulation; respiration by gills; the proboscis gland excretes. Formerly placed in Chordata, they are now a separate non-chordate phylum. Examples: Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus.

sections.heading: 4. Chordata: notochord and the three subphyla
sections.body_md:
Chordates have four **fundamental features** at some stage of life: (1) a **notochord**, a mesodermal rod on the dorsal side; (2) a **dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord**; (3) **paired pharyngeal gill slits**; and (4) a **post-anal tail**. The heart is **ventral**, with a closed circulation. Non-chordates have a ventral, solid, double nerve cord, no notochord and a dorsal heart, if any.

| Subphylum | Notochord | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Urochordata** (tunicates) | Present only in the **larval tail** | *Ascidia*, *Salpa*, *Doliolum* |
| **Cephalochordata** | Extends from head to tail and **persists through life** | *Branchiostoma* (amphioxus, lancelet) |
| **Vertebrata** | **Replaced by a vertebral column** in the adult | fishes to mammals |

Vertebrates also have a **ventral muscular heart** with two, three or four chambers, a **paired** excretory kidney system, and paired appendages (fins or limbs). Hemichordata, though once included, are now treated as non-chordates.

key_terms.definition_md: A mesodermal rod on the dorsal side of the embryo, supporting the body of a chordate.
Paired openings of the pharynx to the outside, present at some stage in all chordates.

sections.heading: 5. Vertebrate classes
sections.body_md:
**Cyclostomata.** Jawless; suctorial, circular mouth without jaws; **6–15 pairs of gill slits** for respiration; body without scales and paired fins; cold-blooded. Marine, but migrate to fresh water to spawn; the larvae return to the ocean. Examples: Petromyzon, Myxine.

**Chondrichthyes.** Marine, cartilaginous skeleton, streamlined body, **placoid scales**, **gill slits without an operculum**, no air bladder (so they swim continuously to avoid sinking), **two-chambered heart**, internal fertilisation, mostly viviparous. Examples: Scoliodon, Trygon, Carcharodon.

**Osteichthyes.** Marine and fresh water; **bony skeleton**; four pairs of gills covered by an **operculum**; **air bladder** regulates buoyancy; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; mostly oviparous with external fertilisation. Examples: Labeo, Catla, Hippocampus.

**Amphibia.** Live in water and on land; **moist skin without scales**; body of head and trunk (tail in some); a **tympanum** represents the ear; alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a **cloaca**; **three-chambered heart** (two atria, one ventricle); cold-blooded; oviparous, with external fertilisation and indirect development. Examples: Rana, Bufo, Ichthyophis.

**Reptilia.** Creeping or crawling; **dry cornified skin** with epidermal scales or scutes; no external ear (tympanum for hearing); **three-chambered heart** (four in crocodiles); cold-blooded; oviparous with internal fertilisation and **shelled eggs**. Examples: Calotes, Naja, Testudo.

**Aves.** **Feathers**; forelimbs modified as **wings**; beak without teeth; hindlimbs with scales for walking, swimming or clasping; **air-filled (pneumatic) bones**; **four-chambered heart**; warm-blooded; oviparous; skin without glands except the oil gland at the base of the tail. Examples: Columba, Corvus, Pavo.

**Mammalia.** **Mammary glands** that nourish the young; **hair**; external ears (pinnae); **four-chambered heart**; warm-blooded; a **diaphragm**; mostly **viviparous**, with unique exceptions (*Ornithorhynchus* lays eggs); heterodont teeth. Examples: Macaca, Camelus, Pteropus.

*Where books differ.* Cyclostome gill-slit numbers are given as 6–15 pairs; individual species have a fixed number (a lamprey has seven pairs). The chapter's arithmetic uses seven pairs for a lamprey and five for a dogfish shark as illustrations.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing "coelomate" for arthropods; the syllabus term is haemocoelomate (the body cavity is a haemocoel).
- Giving only two features for a phylum when five are asked.
- Calling an adult starfish bilateral; the adult is radial and the larva is bilateral.
- Saying all reptiles have a three-chambered heart; crocodiles have four chambers.
- Placing Hemichordata among the chordates.
- Forgetting the **ventral heart** and the **post-anal tail** in the features of a chordate.
- Writing that bats are birds because they fly; they are mammals.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a phylum or class name, a term, an example, a give-a-reason.
- 2- and 3-mark questions: differences between two phyla or classes, features of one phylum, three features with two examples.
- 5-mark questions in parts: distinguishing features of several phyla in a table, the fundamental features of chordates with a labelled figure, a comparison of vertebrate classes.

questions.stem_md: A diver finds a marine animal with five identical arms around a central disc. It can be cut into two equal halves by several different vertical planes through the centre. The animal is

options.text_md: biradial only, with a single plane

questions.solution_md: More than one plane through the central axis gives equal halves: radial symmetry — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An embryologist finds that an embryo has only an outer and an inner layer of cells with a jelly-like layer between them. The adult will be
questions.solution_md: Two germ layers with mesoglea between them mean a diploblastic animal such as a cnidarian — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student cuts the body of an animal and finds that both the outer rings and the internal organs, such as nephridia, repeat in each segment. This condition is
questions.solution_md: Repetition of segments and internal organs is metamerism, typical of annelids — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In which pair of phyla do cells do the same work grouped as tissues, but there are no organs?
questions.solution_md: Cnidaria and Ctenophora are at the tissue level; sponges are cellular and flatworms have organs — option (c).

questions.stem_md: From the list Porifera, Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Echinodermata and Hemichordata, how many phyla are triploblastic?
questions.solution_md: Porifera has no true germ layers and Cnidaria and Ctenophora are diploblastic; the other 7 (7) are triploblastic.

questions.stem_md: Among the same ten phyla, how many are segmented (show metamerism)?
questions.solution_md: Only Annelida and Arthropoda are segmented, so the answer is 2; Mollusca, Nematoda and the rest are not.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The body cavity of an arthropod is not a true coelom.

**Reason (R):** The cavity of an arthropod is filled with blood and is called a haemocoel.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A, since a blood-filled haemocoel is a reduced coelom — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Cnidarians are called diploblastic animals.

answer.model_answer_md: Their body wall has only **two germ layers**, the **ectoderm and endoderm**, with a jelly-like mesoglea between them.

questions.solution_md: Two germ layers.

questions.stem_md: A sponge is called asymmetrical but a sea anemone is radially symmetrical. Explain the difference in terms of planes that divide the body.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **sponge** no plane through the body can divide it into **equal halves**, so it is **asymmetrical**. In a **sea anemone** any plane passing through the **central axis** gives **two equal halves**, so it is **radially symmetrical**.

questions.solution_md: Planes through the axis.

marking_scheme.step: No plane gives equal halves: sponge
Any plane through the axis: radial

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a pseudocoelom from a true coelom, naming one phylum that has each.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **pseudocoelom** (Nematoda) the cavity lies between the body-wall mesoderm and the endoderm, so it is **not fully lined by mesoderm**. In a **true coelom** (Annelida) the cavity is **lined by mesoderm on both sides**, the body wall and the gut.

questions.solution_md: Mesoderm lining.

marking_scheme.step: True coelom described with a phylum

questions.stem_md: An animal has bilateral symmetry and three germ layers, its body cavity is a haemocoel, and its body is segmented. Name its phylum and justify each feature in one line each.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a member of **Arthropoda**. **Bilateral symmetry** gives left and right halves; **three germ layers** make it triploblastic; its cavity is a **haemocoel filled with blood**, not a true coelom; and its body shows **segmentation**, usually fused into head, thorax and abdomen.

questions.solution_md: Arthropoda with the four features.

questions.stem_md: Which cells of a sponge are responsible for creating the current of water through its body?
questions.solution_md: Flagellated collar cells (choanocytes) lining the spongocoel drive the water current — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A colony of Obelia contains sessile, branching polyps that bud off tiny free-swimming medusae, and the medusae shed gametes. This alternation of two body forms is called
questions.solution_md: Alternation of the polyp and medusa forms is metagenesis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which cells on the tentacles of a cnidarian are used for defence and for the capture of prey?
questions.solution_md: Cnidoblasts (stinging cells) give the phylum its name — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A flat, ribbon-like worm from the intestine of a person has a head with hooks and suckers and excretes through flame cells. It belongs to the phylum
questions.solution_md: Hooks, suckers and flame cells in a flat parasite point to Platyhelminthes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A cylindrical worm has a cuticle, a complete alimentary canal with mouth and anus, and separate male and female individuals. Its body cavity is
questions.solution_md: Such a worm belongs to Nematoda, which is pseudocoelomate — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A transparent marine animal glows faintly in the dark and swims by the beating of eight external rows of ciliated plates. It lacks stinging cells. It belongs to
questions.solution_md: Eight rows of comb plates and bioluminescence identify Ctenophora — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined comb jelly has 8 rows of comb plates, and each row has 35 plates. How many comb plates does it have in all?
A pond net collects 48 animals: 6 flatworms, 4 roundworms, 10 annelids, 14 molluscs and 14 arthropods. How many of them are segmented?
questions.solution_md: Only annelids and arthropods are segmented: 10 + 14 = 24.

questions.stem_md: In the same pond sample of 48 animals, what percentage are acoelomate flatworms?

**Assertion (A):** Sponges are placed at the cellular level of organisation.

**Reason (R):** The cells of a sponge are grouped into well-defined organs and organ systems.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: sponge cells are not grouped into true tissues. R is false because there are no organs — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Obelia has a polyp stage and a medusa stage. State one difference between the two forms and name the phenomenon.

answer.model_answer_md: The **polyp** is **sessile and cylindrical**, whereas the **medusa** is **free-swimming and umbrella-shaped**. Their regular alternation in one life cycle is called **metagenesis**, and the medusa makes the gametes while the polyp reproduces by budding.

questions.solution_md: Difference and metagenesis.

questions.stem_md: A parasite found in the liver of a sheep is flat and has no anus. State two features that place it in Platyhelminthes.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **dorsoventrally flattened** and **acoelomate** with **bilateral symmetry**. Parasitic forms have **hooks or suckers** and excrete through **flame cells**, and the gut has a single opening.

questions.solution_md: Any two features.

questions.stem_md: Write two ways in which a roundworm differs from a flatworm in its digestive system and body cavity.

answer.model_answer_md: A roundworm has a **complete alimentary canal** with mouth and anus, whereas a flatworm has a gut with **one opening** or none. A roundworm has a **pseudocoelom**, whereas a flatworm is **acoelomate**.

questions.solution_md: Gut and cavity.

questions.stem_md: State three distinguishing features of phylum Cnidaria and give two examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Radial symmetry**, **diploblastic** body at the **tissue level**.
2. **Cnidoblasts** on the tentacles for defence, anchorage and capture of prey.
3. A **gastrovascular cavity** with one opening, and two forms, **polyp and medusa**.
Examples: ***Hydra*** and ***Aurelia***.

questions.solution_md: Three features and examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe how water moves through a vase-shaped sponge and name the structures involved at each stage.

answer.model_answer_md: Water enters through the many **ostia** in the body wall, passes into the central **spongocoel**, and leaves through the **osculum**. The current is driven by the beating flagella of the **choanocytes** lining the cavity, which also trap food particles; the water brings **oxygen** and carries away **wastes**.

questions.solution_md: Path with structures.

questions.stem_md: Describe three features of a flatworm such as a tapeworm that are adaptations to a parasitic life.

answer.model_answer_md: A tapeworm has **hooks and suckers** to hold on to the host's intestine, a **flat body** with a large surface for absorbing digested food, and **very high reproductive capacity**, with many eggs, so that some reach new hosts. It needs no complex gut of its own.

questions.solution_md: Three adaptations.

(b) **Acoelomate:** no body cavity, mesoderm fills the space (Platyhelminthes). **Pseudocoelomate:** a cavity not fully lined by mesoderm (Nematoda). **Coelomate:** a true coelom lined by mesoderm on both sides (Annelida).

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the water vascular system of a starfish.

answer.model_answer_md: The water vascular system with its **tube feet** helps in **locomotion** and in the **capture and handling of food**. It also assists in **respiration**.

questions.solution_md: Any two functions.

questions.stem_md: Name the locomotory structures of an earthworm and of Nereis, and state the type of excretory organ that both have.

answer.model_answer_md: An earthworm moves with **setae**, whereas *Nereis* moves with lateral **parapodia**. Both excrete through **nephridia**, which are coiled tubes repeated in the segments of the body and open to the outside.

questions.solution_md: Setae, parapodia, nephridia.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A bat is classified as a mammal although it flies.

answer.model_answer_md: It has **mammary glands and hair** and gives birth to young, which it suckles; flight does not decide its class.

questions.solution_md: Mammary glands and hair.

questions.stem_md: Describe the body of a mollusc with reference to its foot, mantle and radula.

answer.model_answer_md: A mollusc has a **soft, unsegmented body** with a head, a muscular **foot** for movement and a visceral hump. The **mantle** covers the hump and usually secretes a calcareous **shell**; the **mantle cavity** holds the gills. The mouth has a file-like **radula** that scrapes food.

questions.solution_md: Foot, mantle, radula.

questions.stem_md: Name three features of arthropods that help them to live successfully on land.

answer.model_answer_md: The **chitinous exoskeleton** protects the body and reduces loss of water. **Tracheae or book lungs** let them breathe air, and **jointed appendages** allow them to walk, fly and feed in many ways. **Malpighian tubules** also save water in insects. Together these features reduce the loss of water in dry air and make a great variety of habits possible.

questions.solution_md: Three adaptations.

questions.stem_md: State three features of echinoderms and explain what is unusual about their symmetry.

answer.model_answer_md: Echinoderms are **marine** animals with a **spiny skin** over a **calcareous endoskeleton**; they have a **water vascular system** with tube feet and **no excretory system**. Their **adults are radially symmetrical** but their **larvae are bilaterally symmetrical**, which suggests that they arose from bilateral ancestors.

questions.solution_md: Features and the symmetry.

questions.stem_md: Explain metamerism and name the phyla in which it occurs, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Metamerism** is the division of the body into **repeated segments**, each repeating some organs. It occurs in **Annelida** (earthworm: externally as rings and internally), in **Arthropoda** (cockroach, with segments often fused into regions) and, internally, in **Chordata** (in the muscles and the vertebral column). Not every phylum shows it: molluscs and roundworms are unsegmented.

questions.solution_md: Definition and phyla.

questions.stem_md: State the function of (i) the operculum and (ii) the air bladder in a bony fish.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **operculum** is a bony flap that **covers and protects the gills** and helps to pass water over them. (ii) The **air bladder** is a gas-filled sac that regulates the fish's **buoyancy**, so that it can rise or sink.

questions.stem_md: A zookeeper states that all reptiles have a three-chambered heart. Correct this statement and say why the heart of a crocodile is more efficient.

answer.model_answer_md: Most reptiles have **three chambers**, but **crocodiles have four**. In a four-chambered heart the **oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix**, so the body receives **more oxygen**.

questions.solution_md: Crocodile exception and efficiency.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a lamprey from a dogfish shark in three ways.

answer.model_answer_md: A **lamprey** (Cyclostomata) is **jawless** with a **sucking mouth**, whereas a **shark** (Chondrichthyes) has **jaws**. A lamprey has **no scales and no paired fins**, whereas a shark has **placoid scales and paired fins**. A lamprey has **seven pairs of gill slits** whereas a dogfish shark has five pairs.

questions.solution_md: Three contrasts.

questions.stem_md: A vertebrate has dry skin with scales, lays shelled eggs on land and has a three-chambered heart. Name its class and explain why it can breed away from water.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a member of **Reptilia**. Its **shelled eggs** resist drying, so they can be laid on land, and **fertilisation is internal**, so no water is needed to bring the gametes together. The **dry scaly skin** also prevents loss of water from the body.

questions.solution_md: Reptilia with reasons.

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between birds and mammals on body covering, reproduction and the structure of the mouth or skin.

answer.model_answer_md: Birds have **feathers**, mammals have **hair**. Birds are **oviparous** (shelled eggs), but most mammals are **viviparous** and **suckle** the young through **mammary glands**. Birds have a **toothless beak**, whereas mammals have **teeth** of different kinds (heterodont) and external ears. Birds also have air-filled bones and wings, which mammals lack, apart from bats.

questions.solution_md: Three differences.

marking_scheme.step: Oviparous vs viviparous and mammary glands

questions.stem_md: Ornithorhynchus lays eggs, yet it is placed in Mammalia. Give three reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Although it is **oviparous**, it has **mammary glands** that supply milk to the young, **hair** on its body and a **diaphragm**. Because these are the defining mammalian characters, it is a mammal and not a reptile or bird. Egg-laying is an unusual primitive feature that it retains.

questions.solution_md: Three mammalian features.

questions.passage_md:
A marine biology class compared five specimens from a rocky shore.

| Specimen | Observations |
|---|---|
| P | Cylindrical, tentacles with stinging cells, one body opening |
| Q | Soft body with a muscular foot and a coiled shell; has a radula |
| R | Jointed legs, hard exoskeleton, blood in open spaces |
| S | Five arms, spiny skin, tube feet |
| T | Many small pores, central cavity, no organs |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) S

**(b)** (b) T then P

**(c)** (i) R belongs to **Arthropoda**. Its body cavity is a **haemocoel**, filled with blood, since the circulation is open.

**OR** (ii) Q is a mollusc. It feeds with a file-like **radula**, and its shell is secreted by the **mantle**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Spiny skin, five arms and tube feet mean an echinoderm — option (a).

**(b)** T is a sponge (cellular) and P a cnidarian (tissue) — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Arthropoda; haemocoel.

(ii) Radula; mantle.

children.solution_md: T is a sponge (cellular) and P a cnidarian (tissue) — option (b).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name the phylum of R and state the name of its body cavity.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Name the feeding organ of Q and the part that secretes its shell.

answer.model_answer_md: Q is a mollusc. It feeds with a file-like **radula**, and its shell is secreted by the **mantle**.
